newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia sniffing around for cargoes of meal-trade.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia sniffing around for cargoes of meal-trade.

text.p: Malaysian buyers are seeking several cargoes of soymeal, but were not in a hurry to conclude a deal on expectations prices will slide further, regional traders said on Thursday.
The rest of the grain and oilseeds market in Southeast Asia was quiet, with most consumers content to kick back their heels and stay out on the belief prices will still come off, the traders said.

"The Malaysians are looking for at least two Handy-sized cargoes of meal. But they're not hurrying to buy because they're still safe as far as their coverage is concerned," a dealer with a European commodity house in Singapore said.
"The Malaysians are definitely sniffing around for some more meal," another dealer in a Western commodity trading company said.
The Malaysians were looking for meal priced at around US$290 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment, traders said. The volume involved may reach anywhere from 50,000 to 100,000 tonnes.
But Indian-origin soymeal for shipment during that period was being quoted in Southeast Asia at about $298-$305 a tonne C&F against about $310 a tonne C&F last week, dealers said.
U.S.-origin meal was being quoted about $5 lower than Indian soymeal and was priced last week at $300-$305 a tonne C&F.
"It's just a matter of pricing," a dealer said.

Singapore traders estimate Malaysia and Indonesia would still need between 100,000-200,000 tonnes of soymeal in early 1997. But their belief that prices would head south may prompt them to delay further buying.

Traders said the recent Thai decision to trim tariffs on imported soymeal, soybeans and fishmeal did not lead to a spurt in purchases because the quota for the year in soymeal of 830,000 tonnes was almost covered.
"Thailand is quiet for now," one trader said.
The rest of the grain market remains subdued with buyers waiting for U.S. corn prices to fall further after a bearish USDA crop report last Friday.
"Corn has no friends in the market right now," a trader with a U.S. trading house said. "The market is still trying to find a level at which to buy."
Another trader said most buyers were convinced that recent price falls will continue and don't want to lock in their positions now and get caught with lower prices later.
"Everybody's seen the prices come down and they believe it's headed lower. But in my experience, it never works out that way," the trader said.

Indonesia and Thailand were well-covered on corn while Malaysia has ample stocks and did not have to buy immediately. In fact, one Malaysian company decided recently to defer talks on 50,000 tonnes of corn for November shipment, traders said.

The price of U.S. corn in Southeast Asia slipped to around $150-$152 a tonne C&F for December/January shipment on board a Panamax vessel against a price of $155-$160 a tonne C&F last week, traders said.
"I think everybody in the region is thinking prices will come down some more. On top of that, most countries are well-covered out to December. There's no sense of urgency to buy," a trader said.
"If you look at Chicago to provide you a few leads, you won't get it at the moment," another dealer said. "It's very quiet right now."
- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
